issues.legal_issue: A constitutional amendment that takes away or abridges fundamental rights is subject to the prohibition against such laws and cannot validly do so.
material_facts: The petitions challenged land-reform laws on the ground that they infringed fundamental rights.
A later constitutional amendment altered the definition of protected land and placed the challenged laws in a constitutional schedule that insulated them from rights-based challenge.
Earlier decisions had upheld Parliament’s power to amend fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that an amendment taking away or abridging fundamental rights is a law within the meaning of Article 13(2) and is void to that extent; Parliament has no power to make such an amendment. The Court overruled the contrary holding in Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India and rejected the contrary view in Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan.
issues.legal_principle: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making a law that takes away or abridges fundamental rights, and an amendment made through Article 368 is subject to that prohibition. Article 368 prescribes the amending procedure; it does not displace the protection in Part III. The Court rejected the reasoning in Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India, [1952] SCR 89, and the contrary conclusion in Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1965] 1 SCR 933. The Court relied on the constitutional scheme protecting fundamental rights and referred to A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha, and Ujjam Bai v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenge: A party challenged a constitutional amendment in a proceeding concerning the protection of fundamental rights.
predicates.amendment_reduces_fundamental_rights: The amendment took away or abridged rights protected as fundamental rights.

issues.definition: When a constitutional amendment is challenged in a fundamental-rights proceeding and it takes away or abridges those rights, the amendment is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may overrule an earlier constitutional decision that it concludes was wrong, while limiting the effect of its new rule to the future to preserve settled transactions.
material_facts: An earlier Supreme Court decision had upheld Parliament’s power to amend fundamental rights, and a later decision had followed that position.
The challenged constitutional amendment and subsequent land-reform measures had been relied on in numerous transactions and had substantially altered agrarian arrangements.
The Court concluded that the earlier rule was wrong but considered retrospective invalidation likely to cause serious disruption.
issues.conclusion: The Court overruled the earlier decision but applied its new rule prospectively, leaving the earlier amendments and transactions based on them unaffected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court adopted prospective overruling for constitutional matters, relying on Articles 32, 141 and 142 and on Great Northern Railway v. Sunburst Oil & Refining Co., Chicot County Drainage District v. Baxter State Bank, Griffin v. Illinois, Wolf v. Colorado, Mapp v. Ohio and Linkletter v. Walker. It held that the Supreme Court may restrict the retrospective operation of a newly declared rule in accordance with the justice of the case, and that the doctrine is available in matters arising under the Constitution and only to the Supreme Court.

predicates.constitutional_case: The proceeding raises an issue arising under the Constitution.
predicates.supreme_court_replaces_earlier_rule: The Supreme Court replaces a rule stated in its earlier decision with a new rule.
predicates.retrospective_effect_would_disrupt_settl: Applying the new rule to past events would unsettle transactions or arrangements made in reliance on the earlier rule.

issues.definition: When the Supreme Court replaces an earlier rule in a constitutional case and retrospective application would unsettle past transactions, the new rule may operate only prospectively.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional amendments made before the Court’s prospective ruling remain effective, so laws protected by those amendments cannot be challenged on the ground that they violate fundamental rights.
material_facts: The challenged land-reform laws had been placed in a constitutional schedule by an amendment that had been upheld under earlier decisions.
The Court limited the effect of its new constitutional rule to the future and expressly preserved the validity of existing amendments.
The petitions sought to challenge the land-reform laws on fundamental-rights grounds.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the challenged laws could not be questioned on the stated fundamental-rights grounds because the existing amendment continued to protect them.
issues.legal_principle: Under the prospective-overruling ruling, the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act and other existing amendments affecting fundamental rights remained valid. As a result, the challenged laws could not be questioned on the stated grounds under Articles 13, 14 or 31. The judgment also discussed the protection afforded by Articles 31A and 31B; Hidayatullah, J. separately considered the challenged laws protected by Article 31A and the President’s assent.

predicates.challenge_to_land_reform_laws: A party challenged land-reform legislation in a proceeding seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.existing_constitutional_protection_cover: An existing constitutional amendment placed the challenged laws within a form of constitutional protection from rights-based challenge.
predicates.prospective_ruling_preserves_existing_am: The Court limited its new rule to future amendments and left earlier amendments in force.

issues.definition: A fundamental-rights challenge to land-reform laws is rejected when an existing constitutional amendment protects those laws and the Court’s prospective ruling preserves that amendment.
